sentences.text: This animal belongs to the genus Echinodon, which contains only one known species named Echinodon becklesii.
The name Echinodon means "prickly tooth," describing a creature that grew to about 60 centimeters in length.
Its skull measured roughly 62 millimeters long and featured one or two canine-like teeth in each jaw, a trait unusual for its group.
The front part of the upper jaw held only three teeth without small serrations, while the lower jaw contained eleven teeth, with the first two being specialized.
The lower jaw was notably deep for a basal ornithischian, reaching a height at its midpoint equal to 30 percent of its total length.
At roughly 60 centimeters long, Echinodon stands as the youngest and smallest known heterodontosaurid.
It possessed one or two canine-like teeth in each jaw, a feature that distinguishes it from other ornithischians.
Sir Richard Owen formally described the genus and the species Echinodon becklesii in 1861.
The fossils were found by collector Samuel Beckles on a cliff at Durdlestone Bay and in the Purbeck Beds near Swanage.
Owen originally identified the first finds as jaw bones and named them Echinodon becklesii.
In 1959, Justin Delair suggested that isolated dermal armor from the Purbeck Beds belonged to Echinodon, though these remains were later reassigned to solemydid turtles.
Research by Sereno in 2012 suggests the primary role of the front tooth row was cropping vegetation, based on wear patterns and jaw movement.
However, Butler and colleagues in 2008 proposed that enlarged canines within the clade served an omnivorous diet, differing from the vegetation-cropping idea.
The animal was initially thought to be a herbivorous lizard before being revised to an intermediate ornithischian.
Richard Thulborn placed it in Hypsilophodontidae in 1971, while Paul Sereno later reclassified it as a member of Heterodontosauridae based on divergent teeth.
Some researchers have occasionally considered Echinodon a basal thyreophore, mainly due to the mistaken association of osteoderms from a turtle member.
This animal lived during the earliest Cretaceous, specifically the Berriasian epoch, approximately 145 to 140 million years ago in southern England and possibly western France.
Sediments from the Purbeck Group indicate a lagoonal environment similar to the modern Mediterranean that became wetter over time.
Currently, there is no evidence linking Echinodon to any specific bed in the Lulworth Formation of the Purbeck Group.
Echinodon was once referred to the clade Stegosauria based on dental anatomy and incorrectly attributed armor that was later identified as belonging to a turtle.
The presence of an arched diastema in Echinodon remains a topic of disagreement among paleontologists.
